title: Competing pathways in polaritonic chemistry and general harmonic environments
authors: Jonas Vinther, Leonardo A. Cunha, Johannes Flick
abstract: Recent experiments suggest that strong light-matter coupling between molecules and cavity modes can significantly modify chemical reaction rates and yields. Despite multiple proposed mechanisms, a clear microscopic understanding of how vibrational strong coupling alters reaction kinetics remains incomplete. Here, we employ a general quantum-dynamical framework for analyzing competing reaction pathways in polaritonic chemistry by considering reaction coordinates with multiple relevant transition frequencies and general harmonic environments. We extend on a tensor-network formulation of the hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) method to compute probability currents between vibrational states, leveraging a concise formulation for effective spectral densities and a controlled compression of Markovian bath modes into system-level jump operators. This allows us to decompose the resulting state-to-state probability currents, revealing how cavity-induced changes in individual transitions propagate through multistep reaction networks. We find that these local modifications can alter kinetic bottlenecks and selectively redistribute reaction flux between competing pathways, changing branching ratios under irreversible conditions without substantially affecting the equilibrium yield in the reversible regime. Finally, for coupled reaction-coordinate, spectator-mode, and cavity environments, we find structured, asymmetric rate profiles arising from interference between hybridized decay channels. Together, these results provide a mechanistic framework for understanding pathway-specific chemical reactivity under vibrational strong coupling.
summary: This paper develops a quantum-dynamical framework using extended HEOM methods to study chemical reactions under strong light-matter coupling. It calculates state-to-state probability currents to show how cavity-induced changes can selectively alter reaction pathways and branching ratios. The findings establish a mechanistic understanding of pathway-specific reactivity in complex quantum chemical environments.
main_problem: The paper aims to provide a microscopic understanding of how strong light-matter coupling (polaritonic chemistry) alters chemical reaction rates and yields by analyzing competing reaction pathways.
main_result: Local modifications induced by cavity coupling can selectively redistribute reaction flux between competing pathways, changing branching ratios under irreversible conditions without affecting the equilibrium yield in the reversible regime.
method: The authors employ an extended tensor-network formulation of the Hierarchical Equations of Motion (HEOM) method to compute state-to-state probability currents.
model_or_system: The system models molecules undergoing reactions (reaction coordinate $\hat{R}$) coupled to spectator modes ($\hat{Q}$) and cavity modes ($\hat{c}$), all embedded in general harmonic environments (baths).
key_observables: Reaction rates, probability currents between vibrational states, kinetic bottlenecks, and branching ratios.
important_parameters: Irreversible vs. reversible regimes, coupling strengths ($\eta_v$), and the spectral density $J(\omega)$ of the bath.
main_assumptions: The reaction coordinate ($\hat{R}$) is assumed to be the only anharmonic degree of freedom, and the bath is treated via the Caldeira-Leggett model.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the physical setup involving coupled modes (R, Q, c) and show the abstraction from the microscopic environment to the full spectral density $J(\omega)$.
paper_structure: The work progresses from identifying the gap in understanding VSC effects to proposing the HEOM extension, detailing the calculation of probability currents, and finally presenting results on flux redistribution and asymmetric rate profiles.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses open quantum system dynamics in chemistry, which is a core area of AMO physics, by providing a detailed, pathway-specific analysis of environmental coupling effects.

The molecule is embedded in a solvent environment represented by a phonon bath (purple). The molecular and solvent degrees of freedom are confined within an optical cavity, represented by a single cavity mode (green).

The couplings between them are denoted by cQ, ηR and ηQ and J(DL) (R,Q,c)(ω) refer to the individual baths which we choose to be of the Drude-Lorentz form.
